mcqs.question: For a genuinely sudden viral spike with no advance warning, what does the answer skeleton rely on, since pre-provisioning isn't possible?
options: Reserved instance pricing negotiated with the cloud provider in advance
A larger peak multiplier applied retroactively to the original QPS estimate
Vertical scaling of the existing database instance to a bigger machine
Autoscaling for what it can catch, plus load shedding once demand outruns it
mcqs.explanation: With no warning, pre-provisioning isn't an option, so the plan leans on autoscaling plus load shedding to protect the core path once autoscaling can't keep up. Reserved pricing is a cost lever unrelated to spike handling, and vertical scaling isn't a real-time response to a live spike.

mcqs.question: Steady-state capacity is 25 servers, and a ticket-drop event is expected to draw 20x normal peak. How many servers should be pre-provisioned ahead of the on-sale time?
options: 45 servers, from adding 20 to the base instead of multiplying
500 servers
125 servers, from applying a 5x multiplier instead of the stated 20x
20 servers, matching the multiplier itself rather than the resulting server count
mcqs.explanation: 25 x 20 = 500 servers is the pre-provisioned target. The other options come from adding instead of multiplying, using the wrong multiplier, or confusing the multiplier with the final server count.

mcqs.question: A viral spike ramps traffic 50x within 90 seconds, against a typical 3-5 minute autoscaling reaction time. What handles the first few minutes of that spike?
options: Whatever capacity already existed before the spike began, plus any load shedding already in place
New instances that autoscaling adds within the first 30 seconds of detecting the spike
An automatic doubling of each existing server's rated QPS capacity during a spike
The cloud provider's own free emergency overflow capacity, provisioned automatically
mcqs.explanation: Since autoscaling takes minutes to react, the entire early window is carried by pre-existing capacity and any load shedding, not new instances. Autoscaling doesn't react in 30 seconds, servers don't gain capacity mid-spike, and there's no free automatic overflow tier.

mcqs.question: Why is over-provisioning for a known, high-stakes launch usually the safer trade despite the wasted idle-capacity cost?
options: Idle servers are never actually billed by cloud providers during low-traffic periods
Autoscaling cannot be configured for predictable events, only for sudden ones
The cost of the system falling over during the moment the business cares most usually outweighs the cost of temporary idle capacity
Pre-provisioned servers automatically convert to discounted reserved pricing, eliminating the extra cost
mcqs.explanation: The trade-off is reputational and business cost of an outage during a critical event versus the bounded, known cost of idle capacity — the latter is usually smaller. Idle servers are still billed, autoscaling works fine for predictable events too, and pre-provisioning doesn't auto-convert to reserved pricing.

mcqs.question: A team says "we have autoscaling, so any traffic spike will be handled automatically." What's the flaw in that belief?
options: Autoscaling only works for CPU-bound workloads, never for I/O-bound ones
Autoscaling requires manual human approval before adding any new instance, on every cloud provider
Autoscaling is always more expensive than pre-provisioning, regardless of spike size
Autoscaling has real lag of several minutes, so a spike arriving faster than that lag runs entirely on pre-existing capacity regardless of configuration
mcqs.explanation: The flaw is treating autoscaling as instant — it genuinely takes minutes, so a fast enough spike outruns it no matter how it's tuned. Autoscaling isn't limited to CPU-bound workloads, doesn't require manual approval by default, and its relative cost depends on the scenario, not a fixed rule.
